sentences.text: Scutellosaurus represents one of the earliest known forms of armored dinosaurs and is currently recognized as the most basal member of this group discovered to date.
This small creature measured approximately 1.3 meters in length, stood about 50 centimeters high, and had a skull roughly 9 centimeters long.
Its protective armor was lightweight, estimated to constitute only one-tenth of the animal's total body weight.
The genus name Scutellosaurus translates to 'small-shelled lizard', combining the Latin word scutellum for 'small shield' and the Greek word sauros for 'lizard'.
Hundreds of osteoderms, or bony plates, were arranged in up to five parallel rows along the neck, back, and extending as far as the tail tip.
These armor plates varied in shape, with some being flat while others were marked with distinct holes.
The animal possessed an unusually long tail that likely served as a counterbalance to its heavy armored body, occupying two-thirds of the total body length.
The vertebral column consisted of six or seven cervical vertebrae, seventeen or eighteen torso vertebrae, five sacral vertebrae, and about sixty tail vertebrae.

In 2008, Richard Butler identified specific distinguishing features, noting that the anterior iliac laminae extend forward while folding into each other and that the tail consists of at least fifty-eight vertebrae.
Modern views describe the head as moderately elongated with a flat top and a pointed snout when viewed from the side.
Originally, Colbert reconstructed the skull as quite convex, assuming it belonged to a primitive ornithischian dinosaur.
The hand claws were small and pointed without a hoof shape, suggesting they were not used for walking.
Scutellosaurus is the most abundant dinosaur species known from the Kayenta Formation.
The tail was enormous, measuring approximately two and a half times the length of the vertebrae situated in front of the sacrum.
A large fourth trochanter on the femur served as an attachment for the long caudofemoral muscle, acting as an adaptation for high speed.
The metatarsals were moderately long with their upper ends closely spaced in a hollow rear arch, a structure typical of a running animal.
The first skeletons of Scutellosaurus were found in June 1971 by David Lawler, an intern at the Museum of Northern Arizona.
The type and only valid species known today is Scutellosaurus lawleri, named in honor of David Lawler, who collected the fossil.
The species name lawleri honors David Lawler, the discoverer of the holotype, while the genus name Scutellosaurus means 'little shield lizard'.
The holotype specimen includes over 300 osteoderms, numerous vertebrae, limb bones, and partial skull fragments.
Its long arms suggest it may have fed on all fours.
It had wide incisors and a row of leaf-shaped, striated cheek teeth adapted for eating plants.
Later researchers doubted Colbert's hypothesis that the animal could walk on all fours.
Scutellosaurus belongs to the parent group Thyreophora.
Scutellosaurus is classified in the class Ornithischia.
Scutellosaurus serves as the nominal genus for the clade Scutellosauridae, a group coined in 1990.
The genus Scutellosaurus was named by Colbert in 1981.
Fossils of Scutellosaurus are found in the Kayenta Formation, which is exposed on the Navajo Nation land in northern Arizona.
